title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimated paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, deterministic execution accounting, the preregistered Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of methodological tradeoffs and threats to validity. (Preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02.)

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore emphasizes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the operational benefit of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures for the chosen generator and prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and paired design: does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect changes relative to applying the same LLM output unchecked on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?
sections.related_work: Empirical surveys and studies show that LLMs produce factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation techniques include retrieval grounding, deterministic validators, and generate–validate–repair loops. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation but typically lack externally auditable, production‑like failure‑rate studies. Architectural proposals recommend combining LLMs with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and guardrail patterns; red‑team audits document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injections that can alter safety outcomes. Our study is positioned as a preregistered, externally auditable measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and sampling policy.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and inferential plan. The preregistration (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals used the bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank with 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge). The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and workflow constraints (valid flag, violation codes, parsed/required command counts). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Adapter and sampling semantics (determinism). The execution model_configuration artifact records the declared model as gpt‑5‑mini and leaves the model parameter "temperature" unset; determinism for the confirmatory contrast was achieved by adapter‑enforced shared_initial generation semantics rather than by asserting an explicit model temperature value. Audit artifacts (deterministic_reconciliation and provider‑call accounting) document that the adapter produced a single shared initial generation per task (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200), ensuring the baseline and guarded conditions compared the identical generator output. Repair policy and handling. Per preregistration, if the primary validator reported violations the system could issue at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM and re‑validate the repaired candidate. Planned exclusions and contamination handling deterministically excluded pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure errors and excluded pairs flagged for validator–emulator disagreement from the primary analysis; sensitivity analyses for alternative treatments were preregistered. Reproducibility note. The run archived all artifacts required for audit (model call logs, validator traces, reconciliation/accounting and bootstrap parameters). We explicitly state a reproducibility limitation: the labeled artifact set does not include the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the 10% Mininet holdout, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of that particular holdout draw even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements for it.
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0, yielding an observed paired difference = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test returns p = 1.0 and bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected failure rate was 0% on this task bank under the frozen shared‑initial generation policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. Repair and contamination checks. No validator failures occurred and thus the repair branch was never invoked; consequently, preregistered secondary estimands about repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failures, and model‑call cost per repair are empty for this run. The preregistered Mininet holdout (randomized 10%, 20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the contamination summary; because the explicit holdout selection seed is not present as a labeled artifact, that zero‑disagreement observation is conditional on the undocumented draw and should be interpreted accordingly. Representative diagnostics. Archived validator traces for representative tasks document nontrivial workflow constraints (labels such as "make_before_break_uplink_switchover", "paired_link_atomic_mtu_change", and "rolling_access_vlan_migration") and show parsed_command_count equaling required_command_count when valid outputs occurred, indicating the benchmark exercised dependency structure despite the universal validator pass outcome.
sections.discussion: Conditional interpretation. The empirical null (zero baseline validator failures) is artifact‑grounded: under the chosen model, prompt policy, and the adapter’s shared_initial enforcement, every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic validator’s checks. This outcome is not a general statement that GVR is always unnecessary; rather, it shows that GVR’s marginal value depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage for the workload and generation policy in question. Methodological tradeoffs. The shared_initial paired design isolates the causal effect of invoking a validator+repair on the identical generator output, but it excludes gains obtainable by re‑sampling or by nonzero‑temperature sampling that might surface failing candidates for repair. For studies intended to estimate unconditional operational failure risk, independent per‑condition multi‑sample designs (or nonzero temperature sampling) should be preferred. Validator coverage and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators codify a set of checks but cannot capture all device idiosyncrasies; the Mininet secondary check is a pragmatic complement but its evidential strength depends on holdout scale and exact reproducibility of the holdout draw. Operational recommendations. Practitioners should (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads under the intended generation policy, (2) expand validator fidelity and emulation checks before relying primarily on automated single‑shot repairs, and (3) consider mixed designs that permit multi‑sample generation and larger repair budgets when baseline failures are nontrivial.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks (gpt‑5‑mini; deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), resulting in an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generator/prompt policy, automated single‑pass repair yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity with larger emulation or testbed checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived under the preregistration id cited above for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Determinism: model_configuration records the declared model and leaves the model parameter "temperature" unset; determinism for the confirmatory contrast was achieved by adapter‑enforced shared_initial generation (adapter accounting documents hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}), not by asserting an explicit model temperature parameter. Execution artifacts and accounting: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; archived artifacts include the execution and analysis bundles (model calls, validator traces, reconciliation/accounting artifacts, bootstrap parameters and contingency outputs). Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement and restarts: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock; no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of that drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
